title: Justify Text to a Fixed Width
statement:
You get a list of words and a line width. Lay the words out as fully justified text, like a newspaper column, and return the lines as a list of strings. Every line must be exactly width characters long.

  • Packing: fill each line greedily. Put as many words on it as fit, in order, with at least one space between neighbours.
  • Spacing: on a line with two or more words, spread the leftover spaces over the gaps as evenly as possible. If they do not divide evenly, the gaps on the left get one extra space each.
  • Single word: a line holding only one word is left-aligned and padded with spaces on the right.
  • Last line: the final line is left-aligned: words separated by single spaces, padded with spaces on the right.

Every word is non-empty, has no spaces, and is at most width characters long.

examples.why: "a bb ccc" is 8 characters, and adding "dd" would need 11. One spare space remains; it goes to the left gap, giving gaps of 2 and 1. The last line is left-aligned.
"justify me" fills the width exactly. "alignment" is alone on its line, so it is left-aligned, not centred.

hints: Handle one line at a time. First decide which words go on the line, then decide how to spread the spaces.
A line from word i up to word j − 1 needs (sum of their lengths) + (j − 1 − i) characters at minimum. Keep adding words while that still fits.
For a middle line with g gaps and S spare spaces, each gap gets floor(S / g) spaces and the first S % g gaps get one more. The last line and one-word lines use single spaces and right padding.

explain.intuition:
This is a careful simulation, and the greedy part is the packing: putting as many words as possible on each line is what the rules ask for, so there is no search. The real work is getting the spacing rules exactly right.

Once a line's words are fixed, the number of spaces is fixed too: width − letters. Divide them over the gaps. Integer division gives the base size and the remainder tells how many gaps, counting from the left, get one extra. The two special cases, a lone word and the final line, skip all of this and just join with single spaces and pad on the right. It is the same problem a text layout engine solves for text-align: justify.
steps: Start at word i. Extend j while letters + words[j].length + (j − i) ≤ width.
If j is past the last word, or the line has one word, join with single spaces and pad the right side to width.
Otherwise, with gaps = j − i − 1 and spare = width − letters, give each gap floor(spare / gaps) spaces plus one extra for the first spare % gaps gaps.
Add the line and continue from i = j.
pitfalls: Giving the extra spaces to the right-hand gaps. They go to the left gaps first.
Justifying the last line. It is always left-aligned, even when it has several words.
Dividing by zero gaps on a one-word line instead of handling it as a left-aligned line.

solutions.title: Greedy line packing
solutions.idea: Pack as many words as fit, then distribute the spare spaces over the gaps, left gaps first. The last line and one-word lines are left-aligned.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def justifyText(self, words: List[str], width: int) -> List[str]:
        lines = []
        i = 0
        while i < len(words):
            j, letters = i, 0
            # with j - i words on the line, one more word needs j - i spaces before it
            while j < len(words) and letters + len(words[j]) + (j - i) <= width:
                letters += len(words[j])
                j += 1
            gaps = j - i - 1
            if j == len(words) or gaps == 0:
                line = " ".join(words[i:j])
                line += " " * (width - len(line))
            else:
                base, extra = divmod(width - letters, gaps)
                parts = []
                for k in range(i, j - 1):
                    parts.append(words[k] + " " * (base + (1 if k - i < extra else 0)))
                parts.append(words[j - 1])
                line = "".join(parts)
            lines.append(line)
            i = j
        return lines

followups: Greedy packing can leave ugly lines with huge gaps. How would you choose line breaks to minimise the total squared slack over all lines? (This is how TeX does it.)
Support words longer than the width by hyphenating them. What changes in the packing step?
